source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Theory: insight problems trigger an initial representation built from prior knowledge. That representation has a low chance of leading to the solution, so the solver hits an impasse. The impasse breaks only when the representation changes. Two change mechanisms are tested: constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition.
numbers: 4 experiments (1A N=20, 1B N=38, 2 N=78, 3 N=34), all matchstick arithmetic with one-stick moves.
limits: Tested on one task family (Roman numeral matchsticks). Authors admit they have no independent evidence that the knowledge is stored as constraints and chunks.
agent_relevance: Gives S6 IMPASSE a mechanism: the stuck state is a bad representation, not too little search. Supports O4 (drop a constraint) and O6 (change representation) as the exits.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Three constraints sit on three representation levels: value (numerals), operator (functional terms), tautology (whole equation). Changing a higher level is a wider revision, so it is less likely to be tried and the problem is harder.
numbers: Problem types: A needs the value constraint only; B needs value and operator; C needs operator and tautology; D needs the value constraint but tight chunks (X to V).
limits: The hierarchy was a design hypothesis fitted to this task. Difficulty is a rank order, not an interval scale (authors say they cannot rank D against B or C).
agent_relevance: A usable ordering for our constraint list: drop surface or value-level assumptions first, then operator-level, then whole-statement assumptions.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Chunk tightness: loose chunks are composite numerals (II, IV, VII) already seen as parts. Tight chunks are I, V, X and the minus sign (single units). Plus and equal signs are intermediate. The chance of decomposing a chunk falls from loose to intermediate to tight.
numbers: Prediction: moves needing tight-chunk decomposition (Type D, X to V) are harder than loose-chunk moves (Type A) at the same constraint level.
limits: Chunk categories were assigned by the authors from perceptual and usage arguments. There was no independent measure of chunk strength.
agent_relevance: In text and code tasks, tight chunks are tokens or idioms the model treats as atomic. A re-representation step should name which units are being treated as atomic.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Experiment 1A: difficulty order in solution frequency was C < B < A and D < A. Block 2 showed no differences among types. Transfer was large for B, C, D and absent for A.
numbers: N=20 (Hamburg students), 5 min limit, 2 blocks of 6 problems. Problem type F(3,57)=7.11, p<.001. Block F(1,19)=14.41, p<.01. Solution times Block 1: A<B (T=12, p<.001), B<C (T=41, p<.05), A<D (T=10, p<.001). Transfer in time: B p<.001, C p<.01, D p<.05, A p=.91.
limits: Small N. Block 2 differences vanished, which fits the theory but also fits plain practice.
agent_relevance: One exposure to the new representation removes the difficulty. After a reformulation works once, the program can store it as a reusable move for later items in the same class.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Experiment 1B replicated the difficulty order with new problem versions, so the effect was not due to specific items. A vs B in frequency missed significance (ceiling effect) while times differed strongly.
numbers: N=38 (Munich), one block. Problem type F(4,144)=10.03, p<.001. No effect of version F(1,36)=0.39, p=.52. A vs B frequency p=.12. Times: A<B T=107 p<.001; B<C T=160 p<.01; A<D T=96 p<.001.
limits: Frequency analysis weakened by ceiling (more than 75% of Type B solved in 1B and 2). Authors lean on solution time to rescue A vs B.
agent_relevance: When measuring a re-representation step, use time-to-solution or tokens as well as pass rate, or ceiling hides the effect.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Experiment 2 asked whether transfer comes from surface similarity or from representational change. Similarity (same problem, same numerals, same order, different) had almost no effect on solution frequency. Transfer size followed initial difficulty instead.
numbers: N=78 (Chicago), 4 similarity groups of 19-20. Problem type F(4,222)=46.45, p<.001. Block F(1,74)=177.97, p<.001. Type x block F(4,222)=39.99, p<.001. Block 1: 96% of Type A and 90% of Type B solved. Similarity effect on time only for Type C (Kruskal-Wallis H=11.05, p<.05); Type D H=6.88, p=.08.
limits: Types C and D were solved faster than A and B in Block 2, a reversal the theory did not predict. Authors gave ad hoc reasons (all numerals equal in one type; a fixed difference of 5 in another).
agent_relevance: Reuse the abstract move (relax this constraint) rather than the surface text of a past solution. A memory of past fixes should be indexed by the constraint relaxed, not by surface similarity.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Experiment 3 is a causal test of constraint relaxation. Tautological versions of Type C were easy, and solving them first removed the difficulty of regular Type C. Type D and Type A were unaffected, as predicted.
numbers: N=34 (18 regular-first, 16 tautology-first). Regular Type C Block 1 solved 61%; tautological Type C Block 1 100%; chi2(1)=12.59, p<.001. Regular-first group Type C 61% to 100% in Block 2, chi2(1)=13.85, p<.001. Type D Block 1: 61% vs 69%, p=.64. Type A: 94% vs 97%.
limits: Ceiling effects blocked the test in the reverse direction.
agent_relevance: An easy sibling problem with the constraint removed can unlock the hard version. Candidate operator: solve a variant without the constraint, then restore it.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Rival explanations were argued against: Gestalt reorganization (no mechanism), variation-selection (cannot say why some moves take longer or why transfer differs), gradual transformation (implausible for single-step problems solved in seconds), functional fixedness (all problems use matches; explains blockage not release), mental ruts (predicts no recovery without a pause, yet solvers recovered), remote associations and differential recall (need extra assumptions).
numbers: Discussion section; no numbers beyond the experiments.
limits: These are arguments, not direct tests. Jones 2003 and Oellinger 2008 later tested rivals directly. Authors concede that the constraint and chunk storage format is assumed.
agent_relevance: Mental ruts predict that only a pause helps. Our scaffold needs no pause or incubation step, which fits schema section 4b.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Eye tracking in matchstick arithmetic tested three predictions: fixations lengthen during impasse; early attention goes to values rather than operators; attention shifts to the crucial element before success.
numbers: N=24 students, 1000 Hz eye tracker, problems A, B, C in random order, 5 min limit. Solved: A 23/24, C 18/24, B 9/24. A vs B chi2(1)=18.38, p<.001; A vs C chi2=4.18, p<.05; B vs C chi2=4.78, p<.05. Median solution time: A 22 s, B 300 s, C 136 s.
limits: Small N, bite bar and recalibration (reactivity checked: rates matched the 1999 study). Only three problem types and three time bins.
agent_relevance: Gives a behavioural signature of a stuck representation: staring, not exploring. In an LLM this maps to near-identical repeated attempts, which code can count.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Prediction 1 held for hard problems: mean fixation duration rose across the solving period in B and C but stayed flat after interval 2 in A. Successful and unsuccessful solvers did not differ in fixation duration.
numbers: 3x3 ANOVA: problem F(2,44)=3.49, p<.05; B and C longer than A (both p<.05). Interval F(2,44)=8.58, p<.001. Interaction F(4,88)=1.54, p=.20.
limits: Longer fixation is also predicted by functional fixedness, mental ruts, Einstellung and progress monitoring, so it alone does not isolate this theory. The authors say so.
agent_relevance: Impasse can be detected from outside, but impasse detection alone does not say which representation to change.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Prediction 2 held: in the first third of solving, long fixations (above the median) fell mostly on values, not on the plus and equal signs. Short fixations showed no such bias. Prior arithmetic knowledge sets what the solver treats as variable.
numbers: Element effect for long fixations F(3,63)=24.02, p<.001; no problem effect p=.42; interaction F(6,126)=2.06, p=.06. Chance was 20% per element (5 elements).
limits: The short and long split is a median split resting on Ballard et al. 1997; reading long fixation as deep processing is an assumption.
agent_relevance: Initial representation bias is predictable from the problem format. The program could list which parts a typical reader treats as fixed and probe those first.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Prediction 3 held: successful Problem B solvers raised long-fixation time on the operators across intervals, ending above chance, while unsuccessful solvers stayed below chance. In Problem C, long-fixation time on the result jumped in the last third only for successful solvers.
numbers: Problem C long fixations: interval F(2,42)=5.31, p<.01; success x interval F(2,42)=5.08, p<.05; success main effect p=.33. Problem B short fixations: success effect F(1,22)=7.09, p<.05 in first two intervals.
limits: Problem C short fixations showed only a marginal success effect (F(1,21)=3.09, p=.09). The pre-solution shift is correlational; looking at an element does not show the constraint was dropped.
agent_relevance: Attention shifts to the neglected element before the answer appears. A scaffold step that forces enumeration of every element, including ones assumed fixed, mimics this shift.

source: Tracing cognitive processes in insight problem solving: GAMs and change point analysis (re-analysis of Bilalic et al. 2019 eye data)
finding: A re-analysis asks whether the pre-solution attention shift is sudden or gradual. Solvers raised dwell time on the critical plus sign late in the first 5 minutes. After a hint (change the operators too) attention moved to the equal sign and then the plus sign. Whether the shift looks sudden depends on the statistical method.
numbers: Data from Bilalic et al. 2019: N=61 (5 male, mean age 22.8), 34% solved unaided, 11% more after hint, 10 time bins. GAM located the change from the 90% bin; quadratic ANOVA from the 80% bin; change-point model near the 90% bin for solvers.
limits: Footnote reportedly says the plotted data were simulated to show a sudden shift and the original data showed a gradual shift. One problem, mostly female sample, re-analysis of old data, results depend on binning. Read through a page summary, not the PDF.
agent_relevance: Sudden restructuring is the weakest part of the theory. Do not build the agent on a sudden insight flip. Treat re-representation as a tried operator, checked by code.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight
finding: Head-to-head test on an unlimited-move car park (sliding block) puzzle where the taxi must be moved before an exit path can open. All 30 eye-tracked solvers had an impasse before the first taxi move, and fixation time on that move exceeded neighbouring moves. Both theories got some support, but manipulations aimed at constraint relaxation moved performance and progress monitoring predicted no change.
numbers: N=39 in 3 conditions of 13 (normal, rotated, easy). 31 solved without a hint, 8 needed a hint (6 in normal). Normal vs rotated/easy solvers: Fisher exact p=0.01. Taxi-move fixation time F(2,58)=5.40, p<.01. Fixation on the right-hand block: solvers 24% vs non-solvers 9% (F(1,39)=6.50, p<.05).
limits: Impasse was defined by the author as fixation at or above mean plus 2 SD. Preprint, not the copy of record. Lookahead split did not match the 64/36 that progress monitoring predicted. Moves and time to solution gave unclear support for either theory.
agent_relevance: Progress monitoring tells when to look for a new representation; representational change tells what changes. A code-side impasse detector plus a constraint-listing step uses both.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight
finding: Non-solvers did move the taxi (5 of 8, about 2 times each) but always put it back. Dropping the constraint in one place was not enough; solvers also noticed the right-hand block needed rearranging.
numbers: 5 of 8 non-solvers moved the taxi before the hint, each returned it. Time in right-hand area at impasse: solvers 19% vs non-solvers 8% (F(1,39)=5.56, p<.05).
limits: Small non-solver group (8). Post hoc interpretation by the author.
agent_relevance: Relaxing a constraint is necessary, not sufficient. After a relaxation the program should re-run search under the relaxed rule, not just note it.

source: Oellinger, Jones, Knoblich (2006) Heuristics and representational change in two-move matchstick arithmetic tasks
finding: Two-move matchstick problems separate representational change from heuristics. The degree of constraint relaxation required drove difficulty; hill-climbing (distance to goal) had minimal effect on solution rates. A partial first move that relaxes the deeper constraint helped more than a value move.
numbers: N=120. Solution rates by type (approximate, from a table): value-value about 90%, hybrid about 75%, operator about 60%, tautology about 25%. Problem type F(1,118)=37.47, p<.001; value-type manipulation F(1,118)=1.54, p>.05. Partial solution type F(1,116)=45.15, p<.001; partial x problem type F(1,116)=6.24, p<.05. Of 509 valid note-field equations: 60.89% value moves, 22.47% hybrid, 16.64% operator.
limits: About 85% of moves reduced distance to the goal, which supports a hill-climbing preference, so both accounts have a part. Rates are approximate values from a table.
agent_relevance: Their model says representational change is the condition for good heuristics to work on the right representation. Order: fix the representation, then search. A hint works best when it hands over the relaxed move.

source: Oellinger, Jones, Knoblich (2008) Investigating the effect of mental set on insight problem solving
finding: Mental set and insight: repeating non-insight set problems did not hurt later insight problems. Repeating insight set problems helped or hurt depending on type. A two-process model is proposed: representational change selects a procedure, proceduralisation then reinforces it and can block a different relaxation later.
numbers: Exp 1 N=108 (no set effects on final solution rates for any test type); difficulty CR3 < CR2 < CR1 (CR3 vs CR2 chi2(1)=32.07, p<.0005; CR2 vs CR1 chi2=9.26, p<.01). Exp 2: controls solved CR3 more than the set group, chi2(1,N=36)=7.26, p<.01. Exp 3: different-procedure group solved more CR1 than controls, chi2(1,N=36)=13.85, p<.001.
limits: Set effects were selective and comparisons used n=36 per cell. The ACT-R style mechanism is speculative and not implemented.
agent_relevance: A practised relaxation is reinforced and can block a different one. If the agent reuses a past fix and it fails, the next relaxation should be a different one.

source: Spiridonov, Erofeeva, Klowait, Morozov, Ardislamov (2026) The modulating role of sources of difficulty in interactive matchstick algebra
finding: Failed conceptual replication of the interactive-matchstick effect (Weller et al. 2011). Participants rarely moved sticks, so the manipulation did not produce interactive solutions. More interactivity raised success for Problem A and lowered it for B and C. Motor movement did not help chunk decomposition and interfered with relaxing operator and tautology constraints.
numbers: Exp 1 N=108, Exp 2 N=90, Exp 3 N=74 (VR). Mean movements Exp 1: A 0.56, B 1.70, C 1.91, D 8.26. Baseline accuracy about 91% (A), 87% (B), 57% (C), 66% (D) in Exp 1. Only VR Interactive Sticks showed a clear effect, about 92% (+6 points). Combined: odds of solving A up 860% (p=.028); odds for B and C down 88% (p=.034, p=.031).
limits: Bayesian logistic regression; credible intervals mostly included zero. Time limit 5 min versus 3 min in Weller.
agent_relevance: More moves or edits is not re-representing. Score a step by whether the representation changed, not by activity.

source: Weller, Villejoubert, Vallee-Tourangeau (2011) Interactive insight problem solving (as reported by Spiridonov et al. 2026)
finding: Second-hand report: Knoblich predictions replicated in the static (2D) group. In the interactive (3D sticks) group, A and B were solved at almost equal rates, and Type C success was 2.5 times the static rate. Read as interactivity neutralising constraint difficulty.
numbers: No figures read from the original; only the summary in Spiridonov et al. 2026.
limits: Original not opened. Interactive condition and interactive solution were conflated, per Spiridonov. Replication failed (previous line).
agent_relevance: Low weight until the original is read.

source: Ohlsson (1992) Information-processing explanations of insight and related phenomena (Keane and Gilhooly eds, Advances in the Psychology of Thinking vol 1, pp 1-44)
finding: Founding formal statement. Poses a double challenge: why people get stuck on problems they know enough to solve, and how they get unstuck. Answer: activation retrieves a misleading representation; impasses resolve by re-encoding, elaboration, or constraint relaxation. Mechanism list taken from the 1999 and 2001 introductions.
numbers: Page range 1-44 confirmed by citations; no numbers.
limits: Full text not found online. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Three exits (re-encode, elaborate, relax) map to O6, an add-information operator we lack, and O4.

source: Ohlsson (2011) Deep Learning: How the Mind Overrides Experience, ch. 4 Creative insight: the redistribution theory
finding: The book recasts the earlier theory as redistribution of activation. Insight events are short and spread through a project (raisins in the dough). Only the listing and chapter opening were seen.
numbers: No numbers. Chapter pages 87-129.
limits: Paywalled; search snippets only. Do not cite mechanism details from it.
agent_relevance: Insights as rare events fit G1 (no scheduled doubt): triggers must come from signals.

source: Kaplan and Simon (1990) In search of insight (as described in Knoblich et al. 2001)
finding: Rival account: the impasse comes from an incomplete initial representation (missing features), so the exit is to notice and encode more, especially invariants, not to drop constraints. Tested on the mutilated checkerboard problem.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Second-hand. Knoblich et al. 2001 note it is unclear which invariants exist in matchstick arithmetic, so the accounts were not separated there.
agent_relevance: Two directions of change: remove a wrong constraint, or add missing structure. A re-representation prompt should offer both.

source: MacGregor, Ormerod, Chronicle (2001) Information-processing and insight: a process model of performance on the nine-dot and related problems (as described in Jones 2003)
finding: Progress monitoring model: solvers hill-climb, compare progress to moves left, and search for alternatives when the goal looks unreachable. Assumed lookahead split 32% one, 32% two, 36% three.
numbers: From Jones 2003: predicted 64% of solvers with lookahead one or two; observed split roughly equal in the car park task.
limits: Second-hand description only.
agent_relevance: Gives a code-side trigger: a goal-distance check against the remaining budget. Pairs with representational change as the content of the switch.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: No runnable model of matchstick arithmetic is given. Computational work cited is on functional fixedness (Keane 1989; Greeno and Berger 1987, unpublished). The theory is stated as rules about the probability of considering a move. The nearest formal sketch is the two-process model of Oellinger et al. 2008 (representational change plus ACT-R style proceduralisation).
numbers: No simulation results in the 1999 paper.
limits: No published runnable model of the full theory was found in the papers opened. Not checked against Ohlsson 2011.
agent_relevance: We could implement the theory directly: constraints as a list the program toggles, chunks as units the program splits. A testable design with no training.

source: Li et al. (2025) Solving Situation Puzzles with Large Language Model and External Reformulation
finding: LLMs asking questions in a long dialogue about a lateral thinking puzzle get stuck on detailed questions or repeat themselves. Fix: end the chat after K questions or a wrong guess, rewrite the puzzle statement with confirmed Q and A facts as hints, and restart a fresh session. Win rate and efficiency improved.
numbers: 5 puzzles, max 30 questions and 5 guesses. Best setting K=5, M=3: 4 wins 1 loss, 2.4 guesses, 22.6 questions, 5 yes, 12.2 no, 5.4 irrelevant. Other column in the same table: 28.6 questions, 3.6 yes, 18.2 no, 6.8 irrelevant (appears to be the baseline).
limits: Only 5 puzzles, ChatGPT only, baseline win count not recovered. Not a matchstick task. Reformulation is external (code restarts the session).
agent_relevance: Direct support for code-driven re-representation: after a failing trace, code compresses verified facts into a fresh statement and restarts. Matches G2 and the S6 to subgoal path.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles Reveal Fundamental Limits of Machine Insight and Self-Evaluation in Reasoning AI
finding: Nazonazo riddles serve as an insight-like benchmark tied to Knoblich 1999 and Ohlsson 1992. Most frontier models stay below humans. Models often produce the right candidate during search but do not endorse it (verification failure).
numbers: 201 riddles; human reference on a 120-item subset, n=126, mean 52.9% (95% CI 46.6-59.2%). 38 LLMs zero-shot: non-reasoning 7.6%, reasoning 17.6% on the 120 subset. GPT-5 within the human CI. Full 201: reasoning odds ratio 2.29 (95% CI 1.99-2.64), accuracy 9.42% vs 19.25%. Verification failures were 5.23% to 39.34% of wrong answers across four models with usable logs.
limits: Riddles are insight-like but not all reasoning. Human sample was a pilot survey. Logs from four models only.
agent_relevance: The bottleneck is recognising the answer, not generating it. Code should test each candidate seen in the trace and select it. Supports G5 and G10; re-representation alone will not suffice without a checker.

source: Orru, Piarulli, Conversano, Gemignani (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in large language models using ChatGPT
finding: ChatGPT solved verbal insight problems about as well as the most probable human outcome. Only the abstract was seen.
numbers: 30 problems from Ansburg and Dominowski (2000), practice and transfer sets of 15 each; human comparison from 20 subjects. Exact scores not read.
limits: Abstract only; model version not stated; public problem set (contamination risk). No matchstick task.
agent_relevance: Do not infer that models already re-represent: verbal insight sets are likely in training data.

source: Korovkin (Yaroslavl State University) Mental schemes in insight problem solving, doctoral summary
finding: Contrasts problem space theory (insight is ordinary search) with representational change (Ohlsson 1992, 2011). Proposes that representation is built from hierarchical mental schemes. Change can be weakening of automated schemes, high-level search for a scheme by analogy, or analysis of contradictions between schemes. Claims executive function load is higher in insight problems.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Doctoral summary; year is a guess from the record. Executive function claim not checked against data.
agent_relevance: A third trigger: find contradictions between two partial readings of the problem. In code this is a consistency check between two representations.
